title: Enterprise Sales Discovery Call: Meridian Health
description: Discovery call with a healthcare prospect surfacing pricing pushback, a security review, and an open Flowline migration risk.

summary.overview: Northwind's Daniel Okafor and Alex Rivera ran a discovery call with Meridian Health's Jordan Blake and Taylor Simmons, who are replacing their three-year-old Flowline deployment after repeated EHR sync failures and the loss of Flowline's roadmap following an acquisition. Jordan pushed back hard on Northwind's list price of $94 per seat, which would put a 450-seat rollout over $500,000 a year versus Flowline's sub-$200,000 cost, and the group worked out a seat-tiered model — roughly 100 full seats plus 350 viewer seats — landing closer to $240,000. Taylor, leading Meridian's first formal vendor security review, confirmed Northwind has a current SOC 2 Type II report, a HIPAA BAA, and Okta SSO with SCIM, but raised an unresolved concern: whether three years of Flowline history can migrate without breaking the audit trail Meridian's retention rules require. The call ended without a decision — Northwind will send a seat-tiered proposal and compliance documents this week, Alex will set up a migrations-engineer session on the audit-trail question, and Meridian's procurement committee still needs six to eight weeks once security clears.

bullet_notes.title: Why Meridian is evaluating now
points: Flowline's API rate limits break the nightly EHR sync roughly twice a month, forcing manual spreadsheet reconciliation.
Flowline's parent company was acquired in June and Meridian can no longer get a roadmap from them.
This is Meridian's first formal vendor security review; it was skipped when Flowline was originally purchased.

bullet_notes.title: Pricing outcome
points: List price of $94/seat/month would put 450 seats over $500,000 a year versus Flowline's sub-$200,000.
Proposed seat-tiered model: roughly 100 full seats plus 350 viewer seats at $18 each, landing near $240,000 a year.
Daniel will send the seat-tiered proposal broken out in writing rather than a single headline number.

bullet_notes.title: Security review and open risk
points: Northwind has a current SOC 2 Type II (renewed March), a signed BAA, and SAML SSO via Okta with SCIM deprovisioning.
Unresolved: whether three years of Flowline history can migrate without breaking the audit trail required for data retention.
Meridian's procurement cycle is six to eight weeks after security clears, with a biweekly committee cadence.

chapters.title: Discovery: why Meridian is looking now
chapters.gist: Jordan frames the multi-vendor evaluation while Taylor and Jordan describe Flowline's sync failures, the parent-company acquisition, and a new formal security review.

chapters.title: Demo: sync reliability and rate limits
chapters.gist: Alex walks through the workspace and shows how queued writes avoid the silent data loss Flowline suffers from; Daniel commits to sending the exact rate-limit numbers in writing.

chapters.title: Pricing objection and seat-tiered math
chapters.gist: Jordan challenges the $500K sticker price against Flowline's sub-$200K cost, and the group works out a seat-tiered model with viewer licenses that lands near $240K.

chapters.title: Security review, SSO, and the audit-trail gap
chapters.gist: Taylor confirms SOC 2 and HIPAA/BAA requirements and SSO via Okta, then raises whether three years of Flowline history can migrate without breaking the audit trail — a question Daniel can't answer on the spot.

chapters.title: Next steps and procurement timeline
chapters.gist: The call closes on a migrations-engineer session, Daniel's seat-tiered proposal, and Meridian's six-to-eight-week procurement cycle, with the audit-trail question still open.

action_items.text: Send the seat-tiered pricing proposal separating full seats from viewer-tier seats
Send the connector rate-limit specs (60 requests/sec, queuing behavior) in writing
Send the SOC 2 Type II report and signed BAA to Taylor under NDA
Schedule the migrations engineer session on whether Flowline history migrates without breaking the audit trail
Confirm the security review committee slot once SOC 2 materials are received

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Thanks for making time this week — I know Thursday afternoons are hard to protect on a hospital operations calendar, so I appreciate you carving out forty-five minutes.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: No problem, though I want to say up front that we're evaluating three vendors in parallel, so I'll be pretty blunt about tradeoffs and pricing as we go.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: That's exactly what I want, blunt is efficient for both of us. Before I show anything, can you walk me through what's actually not working for you today?

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Sure. We've been on Flowline for about three years now. It technically still does project tracking, but honestly nobody on my team trusts the data in it anymore.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: I'll add the technical side of that. Flowline's API rate limits break our nightly sync with the EHR reporting pipeline roughly twice a month, and when that happens someone ends up reconciling everything by hand in a spreadsheet.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: That's a good gut check for us, because reliability under load is exactly one of the things I want to show you today rather than just talk about in the abstract.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Before Alex drives the demo, Jordan, I want to understand the actual trigger for looking now. Three years is a long time to tolerate a tool nobody trusts.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Budget renewal lands in October, and frankly Flowline's parent company got acquired back in June. Nobody over there can tell us what their roadmap even looks like anymore.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: And I've personally been asked to lead a proper vendor security review this time around, which we honestly skipped entirely when we first bought Flowline three years ago.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Good, let's put that on the agenda directly instead of bolting it on at the end like people usually do. Alex, can you take us through the workspace and reporting flow?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Happy to. I'm sharing my screen now — this is a workspace configured to look like a mid-size healthcare ops team, not our polished marketing demo environment.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: The piece Jordan mentioned — sync reliability — comes from us queuing writes instead of dropping them whenever a downstream system is slow or temporarily unreachable. Nothing just silently disappears.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Okay, that directly answers the Friday-afternoon problem we've been living with. What's the actual rate limit on your side if we're pushing data from an EHR integration?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: For the enterprise tier it's sixty requests a second per workspace, and above that it queues rather than rejects outright. I can get you the exact numbers in writing today.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: Please put that in writing, because 'sixty requests a second' needs to survive contact with our actual integration engineer, not just a sales call slide.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Noted — I'll have the connector specs and the rate-limit documentation in the follow-up email tonight, not just a verbal number from this call.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Let's talk price then, because this is exactly where Flowline was cheap and I need to understand why yours isn't before we go any further.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Fair question. Our enterprise tier is ninety-four dollars per seat per month, billed annually, and that includes the integration connectors Alex just showed you.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Ninety-four dollars times four hundred and fifty seats is over five hundred thousand dollars a year. Flowline was under two hundred thousand fully loaded, all in.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: That's a fair comparison to make, and I won't pretend it's the same number. Where the math usually changes is that not all four fifty of your people need a full seat.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Right — a lot of our healthcare customers put clinical staff on a read-only viewer tier, which is priced separately, and only license the ops and reporting users at the full rate.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Okay, how many of our four fifty would actually need a full seat in your experience, realistically?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: For a team your shape, usually somewhere between eighty and a hundred and twenty full seats, with the rest riding on viewer licenses at eighteen dollars each.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: So if we run that math — a hundred full seats plus three fifty viewer seats — it lands closer to two hundred and forty thousand a year, not five hundred.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: That's a very different conversation than the one I walked in with. I'll want that broken out in writing too, because I do not want to present five hundred thousand internally and get corrected later in front of finance.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Understood — I'll send a seat-tiered proposal, not a scary headline number, and I'll break out clinical viewer seats from operational full seats explicitly.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: Before we get too excited about pricing, I need to raise security. We're a covered entity, so do you currently have a valid SOC 2 Type Two report?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: We do, renewed this past March, and I can get it over to you under NDA today. We're also HIPAA-ready, and we have a signed BAA available on request.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: Good, that's table stakes for us, but I still need it in hand before my review board will even schedule a session. Do you support SSO through Okta specifically?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Yes, SAML-based SSO through Okta is included at the enterprise tier, along with SCIM provisioning, so terminated employees get deprovisioned automatically instead of someone remembering to do it manually.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: That automatic deprovisioning matters a lot to auditors, honestly. One open question though — can we migrate three years of Flowline history without breaking the audit trail? Retention rules apply to a lot of that data.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: That's honestly the one question I can't answer with full confidence today. Migration tooling exists, but preserving a chain-of-custody audit trail across two different systems isn't something I want to promise casually.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: I actually appreciate you not just saying yes to make me happy. But that's a real blocker for us — if we can't prove the trail survived the move, compliance will not sign off, regardless of the price we land on.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Let me pull in our migrations engineer for a dedicated technical session specifically on that, rather than have me guess at the answer in front of you right now.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Agreed. So separate from that technical answer, where does this leave procurement timing on your side realistically?

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Our procurement cycle runs six to eight weeks once a vendor clears security review, and our committee only meets every other Thursday, so the calendar matters as much as the content.

segments.speaker: Taylor Simmons
segments.text: I can get the security review itself moving faster if the SOC 2 report and the BAA land this week, but I am not going to shortcut the review to hit a date.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: That's fair, and I would rather this take the right amount of time than get fast-tracked and revisited later by your legal team. Let me summarize where we landed today.

segments.speaker: Daniel Okafor
segments.text: Seat-tiered pricing proposal from me by tomorrow, the connector rate-limit specs in writing, and the SOC 2 report and BAA over to Taylor today under NDA.

segments.speaker: Jordan Blake
segments.text: Let's do that. Honestly the migration answer and the security packet are what determines whether this even reaches committee at this point, more than the price does.
